title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people correctly for the time of day and for the gender of the person you're greeting, say your name, ask how someone is, and face the first surprise: Icelandic verbs change with the person.
bekal: greet with *halló*, *sæll/sæl*, *góðan daginn*, and *gott kvöld*, each in its right place
say your own name with *ég heiti* and ask other people theirs
put together the six forms of *vera* — the only verb you really must memorize in this unit

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fyrsti dagurinn í skólanum
dialogs.intro: The first day of a language course at a school in Reykjavík. Two new students sit side by side before class begins.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Halló! Ég heiti Anna. Hvað heitir þú?
lines.id: Hello! I'm Anna. What's your name?
lines.literal: hello! I am-called Anna. what are-called you?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Hi, Anna! My name is Budi.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Gaman að kynnast þér! Hvernig hefur þú það?
lines.id: Nice to meet you! How are you?
lines.literal: fun to get-acquainted with-you! how have you it?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég hef það gott, þakka þér fyrir. Og þú?
lines.id: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
lines.literal: I have it good, thank you for. and you?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Allt gott! Ert þú nýr hér?
lines.id: All good! Are you new here?
lines.literal: all good! are you new here?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, ég er nýr. Ég er frá Indónesíu.
lines.id: Yes, I'm new. I'm from Indonesia.
lines.literal: yes, I am new. I am from Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, ég er stúdent. Ertu Íslendingur?
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. Are you Icelandic?
lines.literal: yes, I am student. are-you Icelander?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Ég er Íslendingur, frá Akureyri. Talar þú íslensku?
lines.id: I'm Icelandic, from Akureyri. Do you speak Icelandic?
lines.literal: I am Icelander, from Akureyri. speak you Icelandic?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Bara smá. Ég skil ekki vel.
lines.id: Just a little. I don't understand very well.
lines.literal: only little. I understand not well.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Það er allt í lagi! Sjáumst á morgun.
lines.literal: it is all in order! see-each-other on morning.

notes: **Sæll and sæl — a greeting that changes with the person you GREET, not the person greeting.** Literally "blessed, happy". To a man: *sæll*; to a woman: *sæl*. Anna is a woman, so Búdí greets her with *sæl*. No other Nordic language demands this, and English has nothing like it — so get used to checking who's in front of you before you open your mouth.

**Hvernig hefur þú það? literally "how have you it".** That's why the answer also uses "have": *ég hef það gott* — "I have it good". Answering *ég er góður* ("I am good") is wrong; it means "I'm a good person".

**Ég heiti is not "my name is".** *Heita* is a verb of its own meaning "to be called": *ég heiti* I'm called, *þú heitir* you're called, *hún heitir* she's called. The word *nafn* (name) doesn't appear at all.

**Ertu = ert þú, shortened.** Everyday Icelandic glues *þú* onto the end of the verb: *ertu*, *talarðu*, *heitirðu*, *viltu*. The long form isn't wrong, it just sounds a little more careful — and in this dialogue Anna uses both.

**Bless comes from the word "blessed".** It's used for goodbye in every situation, from the cashier to your boss. For a more formal goodbye there's *vertu sæll* (to a man) and *vertu sæl* (to a woman) — the same greeting, used for parting.

**Here is the first surprise: the verb CHANGES with the person.** *Ég er*, *þú ert*, *hún er*, *við erum*. Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish have dropped these changes completely; Icelandic has kept them intact since the age of the sagas. Six forms for one verb — and that goes for every verb, not just this one.

grammars.title: Vera — the verb "to be"
body: The first verb you must master, and the most irregular of them all. The good news: after *vera*, almost every other verb follows a neat pattern.
after: ⚠️ **Three words for "they".** *Þeir* if they're all men, *þær* if they're all women, *þau* if mixed or if you're talking about neuter things. English gets by with one word; here you have to look first at who is meant.
**The pronoun may NOT be dropped**, unlike in Spanish or Italian. *Er stúdent* on its own means nothing; it has to be *ég er stúdent*.
The form *þið eruð* ends in the letter **ð**. It sounds like "eh-rüdh" — soft, almost a hum, not a hard "d".

grammars.title: Asking questions: just swap the order
body: Icelandic has no question word like "do" or "does". A statement becomes a question by **moving the verb in front of the subject** — and nothing else changes.
after: If there's a question word (*hvað*, *hver*, *hvernig*, *hvaðan*), it sits at the very front and the verb stays in second place: *Hvað heitir þú?* — not *Hvað þú heitir?*
This "verb in second place" rule works throughout Icelandic and you'll meet it again in every unit. It is the one word-order rule that is never broken.

sections.title: Greeting by the clock and by the person

blocks.text: Icelandic chooses a greeting by the time of day **and** by who is being greeted. Getting it wrong isn't a grammar mistake but a social one — and that is even more noticeable.

blocks.title: Watch out for two things
items: *Góða nótt* is **not** an evening greeting. It's used only when parting for the night, like "good night" in English. Greeting someone with *góða nótt* as you walk into a restaurant will earn you a puzzled smile — use *gott kvöld*.
To two or more people, *sæll/sæl* changes too: *sælir* (all men), *sælar* (all women), *sæl* (mixed). When in doubt, use *halló* — it's never wrong.

sections.title: Eight first sentences to have ready

blocks.text: These eight sentences cover nine out of ten needs on your first day in Reykjavík. Memorize the sound, not the spelling — and say each one out loud ten times before moving on to Unit 2.

Turn these into questions by swapping the order.
Choose the right greeting. Write one word or one phrase.
items: You walk into a bakery at eight in the morning. To the baker you say ____.
You greet Anna, a female classmate, warmly. You say ____.
You greet Jón, a male classmate, warmly. You say ____.
You walk into a restaurant at eight in the evening. To the waiter you say ____.
You say goodbye to the cashier at the supermarket. You say ____.
